item.title: Patient Experiences of Disrespectful or Judgmental Language in Medical Records
item.dc:creator: Natasha Steele
Amrapali Maitra
Zhiyong Dong
Deborah Wachenheim
Vishnu Nair
Alfredo Reyes-Guzman
Aditya Narayan
Erika Schillinger
item.description:
Authors: Natasha Steele, Amrapali Maitra, Zhiyong Dong, Deborah Wachenheim, Vishnu Nair, Alfredo Reyes-Guzman, Aditya Narayan, Erika Schillinger, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638695
Abstract: Importance The 21st Century Cures Act made clinical notes broadly accessible to patients. However, the frequency and patient-perceived consequences of disrespectful or judgmental language (DJL) in medical records among the general US population remain unknown. Objectives To (1) quantify the frequency of participant-reported DJL in medical records; (2) characterize patient-anticipated consequences; and (3) examine factors associated with DJL and documentation trust in clinicians. Design, Setting, and Participants Cross-sectional, nationally weighted survey of 500 US adults conducted from November 21 to December 4, 2025, using YouGov’s nonprobability-based online panel. Main Outcomes and Measures Descriptive statistics characterized experience of DJL in medical records (patient portal users) or health care (nonportal users) and patient-anticipated consequences. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% CIs were estimated using multivariable logistic regression including sociodemographics and clinical factors for 2 outcomes: DJL and documentation trust. Results Among 500 respondents (mean [SE] age, 48.0 [0.9] years; 253 [51.0%] women, 53 [11.0%] Black, 80 [18.0%] Hispanic [any race], and 315 [60.0%] White, 358 portal users [71.2%]), a total of 83 participants reported DJL: 58 of 358 (17.1%) portal users in their own medical records and/or that of a loved one, and 25 of 142 nonportal users (15.6%) in health care encounters. Patient-reported consequences included 377 of 500 respondents (74.7%) who anticipated DJL would influence subsequent care from a new clinician, and 373 (73.3%) who anticipated worse health outcomes, such as wrong medication prescribing or diagnostic errors. Furthermore, 435 of 500 respondents (85.5%) anticipated they would be less likely to return to the clinician. In adjusted analyses, patients who reported low income (compared with high income: aOR, 2.64; 95% CI, 1.18-5.91; P = .03) had a greater likelihood of reporting DJL, as did those with a diagnosis of chronic pain (compared with no diagnosis of chronic pain: aOR, 3.25; 95% CI, 1.46-7.26; P = .004). The experience of DJL was associated with diminished documentation trust in clinicians (aOR, 5.76; 95% CI, 2.90-11.46; P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions and Relevance In this survey study, 1 in 6 US adults reported DJL in medical records (or in health care experiences for nonportal users), disproportionately affecting those with low income or chronic pain, and DJL was associated with diminished clinician documentation trust. Patient-anticipated consequences such as diminished intent to return to clinician suggest important quality of care and system-level implications. Realizing the promise of health information transparency will require concurrent reform in respectful language in clinical documentation and health care encounters.

item.title: Trends in Violence Against Children in Australia
item.dc:creator: Lucinda Grummitt
Siobhan O’Dean
Tim Slade
item.description:
Authors: Lucinda Grummitt, Siobhan O’Dean, Tim Slade
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638285
Abstract: Importance Administrative data are commonly used to monitor multiple forms of violence against children, within and external to the family, yet different systems capture distinct thresholds of harm. Reliance on single data sources may obscure population-level trends. Objective To examine trends in multiple indicators of children’s exposure to violence in Australia from 2014 to 2024 and to assess whether trends differ across police, health, and child protection data sources. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used a time-trend analysis of Australian national administrative data spanning from 2014 to 2024. Data sources included national police-recorded assaults, hospitalizations, and child protection data from 3 Australian national agency databases. Participants were children aged 0 to 17 years, disaggregated by sex and age group. Analyses were conducted from January to April 2026. Exposures Year, modeled continuously. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were annual rates per 100 000 population on police-recorded sexual assault, family and domestic violence (FDV)–related assault, hospitalizations for assault, and child maltreatment substantiations. Temporal trends were modeled using quasi-Poisson regression with population offsets, and average annual percentage changes were estimated. Turning points were assessed using Davies test and segmented regression. Results Annual population denominators ranged from 2.6 to 2.8 million girls and 2.7 to 3.0 million boys aged 0 to 17 years. Police-recorded sexual assault rates increased steadily among girls aged 0 to 9 years (2.8% per year; 95% CI, 2.0% to 3.6% per year) and those aged 10 to 17 years (4.2% per year; 95% CI, 3.4% to 5.0% per year). Among boys aged 10 to 17 years, rates accelerated sharply after 2021 (15.7% per year; 95% CI, 5.5% to 26.9% per year). FDV-related assault showed a similar trend, with stable to modest increases before 2021 followed by steep increases thereafter. Assault-related hospitalizations were generally stable, except for declines among boys aged 10 to 17 years (−1.4% per year; 95% CI, −2.7% to −0.1% per year). Overall child maltreatment substantiation remained stable, but declines were found for physical (−3.2% per year; 95% CI, −5.2% to −1.2% year) and sexual (−3.6% per year; 95% CI, −5.2% to −2.0% per year) abuse, alongside an increase in emotional abuse substantiations to 2020 (7.6% per year; 95% CI, 5.2% to 10.0% per year), followed by a decline (−7.0% per year; 95% CI, −11.8% to −1.9% per year). Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study using Australian national administrative data, trends in violence against children differed substantially across systems. Although police data indicated increased violence exposure, particularly in recent years, child-protection substantiations and hospitalizations remained stable or declined. Strengthened national surveillance is critical.

item.title: Thrombectomy for Acute Stroke Due to Medium Vessel Occlusion Across Perfusion Mismatch Profiles
item.dc:creator: Umberto Pensato
Gunjan Jindal
William Diprose
Aravind Ganesh
Pattarawut Charatpangoon
Ethan MacDonald
Alexander Stebner
Salome Bosshart
item.description:
Authors: Umberto Pensato, Gunjan Jindal, William Diprose, Aravind Ganesh, Pattarawut Charatpangoon, Ethan MacDonald, Alexander Stebner, Salome Bosshart, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638823
Abstract: Importance Recent trials have not demonstrated a benefit of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) over medical therapy in acute stroke due to medium vessel occlusion (MeVO). However, it remains uncertain whether selected patients with favorable perfusion may benefit from EVT. Objective To investigate the association between perfusion mismatch profiles and functional outcomes in MeVO stroke and to determine whether these profiles modify the effect of EVT. Design, Setting, and Participants This study was a post hoc analysis of ESCAPE-MeVO (Endovascular Treatment to Improve Outcomes for Medium Vessel Occlusion), a multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted in North America, Europe, and the United Kingdom between April 2022 and June 2024, with a 90-day follow-up. Trial participants included patients with acute MeVO stroke presenting within 12 hours from last known well and evidence of salvageable brain tissue. This analysis included only patients with interpretable baseline perfusion imaging. Data were analyzed from March to July 2026. Interventions Randomization to EVT plus usual care vs usual care alone. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was the 90-day ordinal modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score. Secondary outcomes included 24-hour follow-up infarct volume and 90-day mRS score of 0 to 1 and 0 to 2. Perfusion mismatch ratio and volume were defined as the ratio and difference between the critically hypoperfused area and the ischemic core, with volume thresholds defined by site-specific postprocessing software. Results Of 530 enrolled patients, 309 (58.3%) had available baseline perfusion imaging and were included in this study (EVT: n = 146; usual care: n = 163). Patient median (IQR) age was 73 (63-82) years, and 141 (45.6%) were women. Median (IQR) perfusion mismatch volume was 37.2 (22.1-57.2) mL, and the median (IQR) mismatch ratio was 6.1 (2.8-10.0). Ordinal 90-day mRS score was not associated with perfusion mismatch volume (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 1.03 [95% CI, 0.99-1.07] per 10-mL increase) or perfusion mismatch ratio (AOR, 1.03 [95% CI, 0.97-1.09] per 1-unit increase). There was no modification of EVT effect by perfusion mismatch volume or ratio on ordinal 90-day mRS. Results were consistent across secondary outcomes and subgroups. Conclusions and Relevance In this exploratory post hoc analysis of acute MeVO stroke, perfusion mismatch profiles were not associated with functional outcomes and did not modify the effect of EVT. These findings suggest that perfusion imaging profiles based on currently used thresholds and cutoffs did not identify patients likely to benefit from EVT in the ESCAPE-MeVO trial. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05151172

item.title: Digital and Coaching Interventions for Uptake of Cancer Genetic Testing
item.dc:creator: Sarah Austin
Emerson Delacroix
John D. Rice
Erika Koeppe
Elizabeth Rizzo
Erika N. Hanson
Liliana Arida-Moody
Shayna Weiner
item.description:
Authors: Sarah Austin, Emerson Delacroix, John D. Rice, Erika Koeppe, Elizabeth Rizzo, Erika N. Hanson, Liliana Arida-Moody, Shayna Weiner, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638274
Abstract: Importance Germline genetic testing (GT) for hereditary cancer risk can inform cancer treatment, screening, and prevention, yet testing rates remain low. Alternative strategies are needed to improve facilitation of GT. Objective To compare 2 patient-level interventions to increase uptake of hereditary cancer GT against usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants The Michigan Genetic Hereditary Testing (MiGHT) randomized clinical trial analyzed self-reported GT outcome data from participants meeting clinical GT criteria between April 21, 2022, and November 21, 2025. Participants were adults (age ≥18 years) who met national criteria for genetic evaluation and had not previously completed germline GT recruited from oncology, primary care, and gastroenterology practices; research registries; and the general public in Michigan. Data were analyzed from April 30, 2025, to May 1, 2026. Interventions Participants were randomized to either telephone-based health coaching, a self-directed digital intervention, or usual care. Both interventions incorporated genetics education and motivational interviewing concepts. Main Outcomes and Measures GT uptake was assessed at 6- and 12-month time points. The primary outcome was completion of GT by 6 months. The effects of study group on GT uptake were evaluated using logistic regression, adjusting for cancer history, age, gender, and race. Results A total of 793 participants (median [IQR] age, 64 [51-71] years; 458 [57.8%] female) were randomized to health coaching (261 participants), the digital intervention (265 participants), or usual care (267 participants). Overall, 31 participants (4.9%) reported completing GT by the 6-month time point, and 76 participants (9.6%) underwent GT across the 12-month study period. Compared with usual care, participants in the digital intervention group had higher odds of completing GT by 6 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.88; 97.5% CI, 1.27-14.80), while those in the health coaching group had higher odds of completing GT by 12 months (AOR, 2.25; 97.5% CI, 1.11-4.77). Participants in the digital intervention group were more likely to express intention to test at 6 months (AOR, 2.36; 95% CI, 1.44-3.93), whereas those in the health coaching group had higher intention at both 6 (AOR, 2.99; 95% CI, 1.83-4.95) and 12 (AOR, 2.29; 95% CI 1.29-4.15) months compared with usual care. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of GT interventions, GT uptake was higher among participants who received the digital or health coaching interventions compared with usual care, although overall testing rates were low. These results underscore the importance of content delivery, motivational messaging, and alternative GT care models. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT05162846 .

item.title: Maternal Prenatal Diet and Colic and Eczema Among Infants
item.dc:creator: Emily Oken
Sheryl L. Rifas-Shiman
Karen M. Switkowski
Kari Nadeau
Jenifer R. Lightdale
item.description:
Authors: Emily Oken, Sheryl L. Rifas-Shiman, Karen M. Switkowski, Kari Nadeau, Jenifer R. Lightdale
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638472
Abstract: Importance Infantile colic is a disorder of gut-brain interaction whose cause is poorly understood. Objective To estimate associations of maternal diet quality and intakes of specific allergenic foods with infant eczema and colic. Design, Setting, and Participants Project Viva prospective cohort of 2128 mother-child pairs unselected for atopic risk with recruitment in early pregnancy in Eastern Massachusetts from April 1999 to November 2002, with follow-up to October 2003, and data analysis November 2025 to July 2026. Exposures Prenatal diet via food frequency questionnaires in early pregnancy (median [IQR], 9.9 [8.8-11.3] weeks) and midpregnancy (median [IQR], 27.9 [26.7-28.8] weeks). The Mediterranean Diet Score (MDS) and Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) were calculated and intake of commonly allergenic foods was determined. Main Outcomes and Measures Maternal report of colic symptoms and eczema diagnosis at median (IQR) of 6.3 (6.0-6.8) months. Results Among 1324 pairs with exposure and outcome data, mean (SD) maternal age was 32.6 (4.6) years, 667 (50.4%) were nulliparous, and 532 (40.2%) reported a history of atopy; 152 (11.5%) infants had eczema alone, 273 (20.6%) had colic alone, and 61 (4.6%) had both. In multinomial logistic regression models adjusted for maternal age, race, ethnicity, education, parity, smoking, and atopy, greater mean (SD) MDS (4.6 [2.0] points) was associated with lower odds of colic and eczema (odds ratio [OR], 0.85; 95% CI, 0.74-0.98 per 1 point), and mean (SD) DII (−2.7 [1.3]) was associated with higher odds (OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.12-1.61 per 1 point). Neither diet score was associated with eczema or colic alone. Seafood intake was associated with lower odds of colic and eczema combined (OR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.58-0.97 per weekly serving). Nut intake was associated with higher risk for colic among those without eczema (eg, OR, 1.05; 95% CI, 1.00-1.09 per weekly serving of any nuts or peanuts), but not with colic and eczema combined (OR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.88-1.07). Dairy or egg intakes were not associated with any outcomes. Associations of dietary scores and fish intake with colic were stronger among infants of atopic mothers. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 1324 mother-child pairs, poorer maternal diet quality and lower seafood intake were associated with infantile colic with eczema or maternal atopic history.

item.title: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Facility Access and Clinical Outcomes Among Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction
item.dc:creator: Yu-Chu Shen
Renee Y. Hsia
item.description:
Authors: Yu-Chu Shen, Renee Y. Hsia
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638687
Abstract: Importance The proliferation of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) facilities across the US has raised questions about whether expanding capacity improves outcomes in areas already served vs those without prior access. Objective To evaluate the association between the opening of PCI-capable facilities and outcomes following acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in communities with and without baseline PCI access. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used California data from inpatient, emergency department, and ambulatory surgery encounters from January 1, 2011, to December 31, 2022, including all adults hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of AMI. Zip code communities were categorized by baseline (2011) access to PCI-capable facilities within a 30-minute drive. Exposure Opening of a PCI-capable facility within 30 minutes of a community’s zip code during the study period. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were (1) admission to a PCI-capable facility, (2) receipt of PCI during the index hospitalization, (3) unscheduled acute care visit within 30 days, and (4) all-cause mortality at 30 days and 1 year. Linear probability models with community and time-fixed effects estimated changes in outcomes following PCI facility openings separately for communities with and without baseline access. Results Among 590 282 patients with AMI (157 435 younger than age 60 years [27%]; 222 773 female [38%]; 63 460 Asian [11%], 129 137 Hispanic [22%], 315 326 White [53%]), 500 778 (85%) lived in communities with baseline PCI access, and 89 504 (15%) lived in communities without; 18 805 patients (21%) without baseline access experienced a PCI opening. Openings in communities without baseline access were associated with a 30.0 percentage point (pp) increase (95% CI, 28.2 to 31.8 pp) in admission to PCI-capable hospitals and a 5.1 pp increase (95% CI, 3.3 to 7.0 pp) in PCI receipt, along with reductions in 30-day (–1.8 pp; 95% CI, –3.2 to –0.5 pp) and 1-year (–2.8 pp; 95% CI, –4.7 to –1.0 pp) mortality. In contrast, openings in communities with baseline access were associated with smaller gains in admission (1.5 pp; 95% CI, 1.1 to 1.9 pp), modest increases in PCI use (1.0 pp; 95% CI, 0.5 to 1.6 pp), decreases in unscheduled visits within 30 days (–0.7 pp; 95% CI, –1.2 to –0.2 pp), and no mortality change. Sensitivity analyses restricted to higher-volume PCI centers (50 annual cases or more) yielded consistent findings. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of 590 282 patients with AMI in California, opening new PCI facilities was associated with substantial improvements in communities without prior PCI availability, including a 53% relative increase in access to admission, 16% increase in PCI use, and 20% and 15% reductions in 30-day and 1-year mortality, respectively. In contrast, already served areas showed smaller benefits and no mortality improvement. PCI expansion should prioritize underserved regions to maximize population-level benefits and avoid inefficient duplication of services.

item.dc:creator: Shahin Sayed
Li Feng
Hela Koka
Manel Haj Mansour
Difei Wang
Maria Brown
Kristine Jones
Margaret Maina
item.description:
Authors: Shahin Sayed, Li Feng, Hela Koka, Manel Haj Mansour, Difei Wang, Maria Brown, Kristine Jones, Margaret Maina, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638664
Abstract: Importance Breast cancer subtyping based on immunohistochemistry (IHC) guides systemic therapy where gene expression profiling assays are unavailable, yet its validity against molecular reference standards remains poorly characterized in African populations, where laboratory infrastructure and access to pathology services are limited. Objective To evaluate concordance between IHC-based breast cancer subtyping and PAM50 intrinsic subtypes in East and West African populations and identify resource-appropriate strategies to improve classification. Design, Setting, and Participants This cross-sectional study included Kenyan (diagnosed 2012-2022) and Ghanaian women (diagnosed 2013-2015) with invasive breast cancer, from whom formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor specimens were collected during the same periods. Gene expression profiling and data analyses were performed between April 2020 and August 2026 for both cohorts. Exposures Tumor subtyping using standard IHC markers (estrogen receptor [ER], progesterone receptor [PR], and ERBB2 status and Ki-67) and histologic grade vs PAM50 intrinsic subtyping derived from a gene expression panel. Main Outcomes and Measures Concordance between IHC-based and PAM50 intrinsic subtypes was assessed using Cohen κ statistics, with sensitivity and specificity calculated against PAM50. Results Among 460 women in Kenya with breast cancer (mean [SD] age at diagnosis, 50.3 [12.5] years), 224 (49.4%) had grade 3 disease and 148 (42.3%) had stage III or IV tumors. A total of 451 women in Ghana with breast cancer (mean [SD] age, 49.9 [12.0] years; 317 [75.1%] with grade 3 disease) were enrolled as a validation cohort. PAM50 classified patients’ tumors as luminal A (201 tumors [43.7%]), luminal B (82 tumors [17.8%]), ERBB2 -enriched (50 tumors [10.9%]), basal-like (99 tumors [21.5%]), and normal-like (28 tumors [6.1%]). Concordance between IHC and PAM50 was highest for basal-like tumors (sensitivity ranging from 73.3% [95% CI, 61.9%-82.9%] to 79.6% [95% CI, 70.3%-87.1%]; specificity ranging from 96.9% [95% CI, 93.9%-98.6%] to 97.3% [95% CI, 94.9%-98.7%]) and moderate for ERBB2 -enriched tumors (sensitivity was 50.0% across all schemes, with 95% CIs ranging from 33.8%-66.2% to 35.5%-64.5%; specificity ranging from 97.6% [95% CI, 95.6%-98.9%] to 97.9% [95% CI, 95.6%-99.2%]). Luminal subtypes showed substantial misclassification using ER, PR, and ERBB2 status alone. Incorporation of Ki-67 (≥20%) or histologic grade improved discrimination between luminal A and luminal B tumors, increasing luminal B classification from 12.2% (95% CI, 8.5%-16.7%) to 41.2% (95% CI, 35.2%-47.4%), even when PR status was excluded from the panel. Findings were independently validated in women with breast cancer from Ghana. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of African breast cancer populations, standard IHC markers performed well for basal-like tumors but frequently misclassified luminal subtypes without proliferation markers. When testing was constrained, proliferation markers contributed more to molecular approximation than PR, with histologic grade providing useful information when Ki-67 was unavailable. These findings support tiered, resource-adapted classification where molecular assays are inaccessible.

item.title: Home-Based Programs and Cardiac Rehabilitation Participation Among Veterans With Ischemic Heart Disease
item.dc:creator: Linda G. Park
Ning Zhang
David W. Schopfer
Amit J. Shah
Abdelaziz Elnaggar
Saron Hunegnaw
Mary A. Whooley
item.description:
Authors: Linda G. Park, Ning Zhang, David W. Schopfer, Amit J. Shah, Abdelaziz Elnaggar, Saron Hunegnaw, Mary A. Whooley
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638356
Abstract: Importance Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a guideline-recommended secondary prevention program that reduces morbidity and mortality among patients with ischemic heart disease (IHD) yet remains underutilized. Over the past decade, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has implemented strategies to increase CR participation, including expansion of virtual home-based CR (HBCR) programs as alternatives to traditional center-based CR (CBCR). Objective To examine temporal trends and factors associated with CR participation among veterans with IHD. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study used national VHA electronic health record data to evaluate CR participation among veterans hospitalized for IHD, identified using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9 ), ICD-10 , or Current Procedural Terminology codes from 2012 to 2022. Data were analyzed from October 25, 2025, to July 25, 2026. Exposures Availability of CR delivery models at Veterans Affairs (VA) facilities, including referral to community care programs only, VA CBCR, or VA HBCR. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was the proportion of eligible veterans with acute myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass graft surgery who participated in any type of CR within 12 months of the index event, identified using Current Procedural Terminology codes and VA stop codes from VA-provided, VA-purchased, or Medicare-claimed services. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with CR participation. Results Among 405 907 veterans with IHD (mean [SD] age, 68.5 [11.1] years; 391 998 men [96.6%]), 63 185 (15.6%) participated in CR. Participation increased from 9.6% in 2012 to 17.1% in 2022, with a peak of 19.7% in 2018. In 2022, participation was higher at facilities offering HBCR (20.0%) compared with those offering CBCR without HBCR (14.8%) or referral to community care programs only (14.3%). The adjusted odds ratio (AOR) of participation among veterans treated at facilities offering HBCR was 1.80 (95% CI, 1.75-1.84), whereas the AOR of participation at facilities offering CBCR without HBCR was 1.29 (95% CI, 1.26-1.32) compared with referral to community care programs only. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of veterans with IHD, participation in CR nearly doubled between 2012 and 2022. Patients who had index events at facilities offering HBCR had higher CR participation than those at facilities offering CBCR without HBCR, or at facilities offering only referral to community care. Broader availability of HBCR programs may help improve participation within large health systems.

item.title: Influenza Vaccination Preferences Among Adults Aged 60 Years and Older in Beijing, China
item.dc:creator: Mengmeng Jia
Yuxi Liu
Jiarui Zheng
Fenghua Su
Jitao Zhang
Mingyue Jiang
Tongsiman Wang
Xinqi Wang
item.description:
Authors: Mengmeng Jia, Yuxi Liu, Jiarui Zheng, Fenghua Su, Jitao Zhang, Mingyue Jiang, Tongsiman Wang, Xinqi Wang, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638674
Abstract: Importance Influenza vaccination coverage among older adults remains suboptimal in China despite free vaccination policies in some regions. Understanding their preferences may inform strategies to improve uptake. Objective To quantify preferences for influenza vaccination attributes and assess preference heterogeneity by prior influenza vaccination history. Design, Setting, and Participants This community-based survey study was conducted at 2 districts in Beijing, China, where influenza vaccination is provided free of charge for adults aged 60 years or older. A convenience sample of adults aged 60 years or older was included from 6 Beijing subdistricts and participated in a discrete choice experiment conducted from August to September 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures Stated choice among 2 hypothetical influenza vaccination profiles and an opt-out option. Attributes included vaccine effectiveness, risk of mild adverse effects, vaccination venue and operating hours, outreach method, information source, and message content. Conditional logit, mixed logit, scenario simulations, and vaccination-history interaction analyses were performed. Results Among 514 participants included in the analyses, the median age was 71 years (IQR, 65-79 years), and 356 (69.3%) were women. Higher vaccine effectiveness was associated with greater vaccination preference (β = 2.12; 95% CI, 1.37 to 2.88), whereas higher perceived risk of mild adverse effects was associated with lower preference (β = −5.53; 95% CI, −7.83 to −3.22). Participants preferred community-based vaccination settings, telephone reminders (β = 1.06; 95% CI, 0.76 to 1.36), information from government or community organizations (β = 0.78; 95% CI, 0.54 to 1.02), and messages emphasizing protection of family members (β = 0.50; 95% CI, 0.26 to 0.74). Increasing vaccine effectiveness from 20% to 80% and reducing perceived risk of adverse effects from 20% to 5% were associated with 30.74– and 19.96–percentage-point (pp) increases in the model-estimated choice probability, respectively. Compared with participants with prior vaccination, never-vaccinated participants had a greater preference for opting out (difference in β = 1.07; 95% CI, 0.11 to 2.03), greater sensitivity to mild adverse effect risk (difference in β per 10-pp increase, −0.49; 95% CI, −0.93 to −0.05), and lower responsiveness to vaccine effectiveness (difference in β per 10-pp increase, −0.18; 95% CI, −0.31 to −0.04). Conclusions and Relevance In this discrete choice experiment of older adults in Beijing, influenza vaccination preferences were associated with vaccine profiles, trusted communication, and community-based service delivery. Prior vaccination history identified differences in benefit-risk weighting that may inform broad and targeted vaccination strategies.

item.title: Depression and Anxiety Risk in Children With Intellectual Developmental Disorder
item.dc:creator: Jimin Clara Park
Ruby Charak
Megan N. Baber
Srinivasa B. Gokarakonda
Angela L. Scott
Kyung Mee Kim
Chung Eun Lee
In Young Cho
item.description:
Authors: Jimin Clara Park, Ruby Charak, Megan N. Baber, Srinivasa B. Gokarakonda, Angela L. Scott, Kyung Mee Kim, Chung Eun Lee, In Young Cho, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638681
Abstract: Importance Population-based pediatric data on depression and anxiety incidence among children with intellectual developmental disorder (IDD), particularly in Asian populations, are limited. Objective To investigate associations between IDD and depression and anxiety incidence and evaluate moderating factors. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used linked data from South Korea’s National Health Insurance Service database and National Disability Registry from 2004 to 2020. Children aged 2 to 17 years with newly registered IDD were matched 1:3 by sex and birth year to children without developmental disorders. Follow-up continued until 2023. Data were analyzed from April 20 to July 9, 2025. Exposure Intellectual developmental disorder among children and adolescents. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was incident depression and anxiety as defined by International Statistical Classification of Disease, Tenth Revision codes. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for developing depression or anxiety were estimated using multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards regression models. Results Among 236 132 children (mean [SD] age, 9.3 [4.3] years; 64.2% male), 59 033 (25.0%) had IDD. Among children with IDD, 20.1% were diagnosed with depression and 21.9% with anxiety at least 1 year after baseline. Compared with children without developmental disorders, children with IDD had higher risk of depression (HR, 2.18 [95% CI, 2.13-2.24]) and anxiety (HR, 1.85 [95% CI, 1.80-1.89]) after adjusting for sex, age, income level, residential location, and comorbidity burden. Compared with children without developmental disorders, risks of depression and anxiety, respectively, were higher among male children (adjusted HR [AHR], 2.46 [95% CI, 2.39-2.54] and 2.06 [95% CI, 2.00-2.12]), younger children (aged 2-5 years: AHR, 2.83 [95% CI, 2.66-3.01] and 2.41 [95% CI, 2.27-2.55]; aged 6-8 years: AHR, 2.51 [95% CI, 2.40-2.64] and 2.12 [95% CI, 2.02-2.22]), urban residents (AHR, 2.36 [95% CI, 2.25-2.48] and 1.97 [95% CI, 1.88-2.06]), and children with a mild comorbidity burden (Charlson Comorbidity Index score of 1) (AHR, 2.32 [95% CI, 2.22-2.43] and 1.98 [95% CI, 1.90-2.07]). Stratification by sex, younger age, and mild comorbidity burden consistently showed higher risks of depression and anxiety across both sexes with IDD compared with children without developmental disorders (all P &amp;lt; .001 for interaction). In males with IDD, rural residence was associated with higher depression risk (AHR, 2.71 [95% CI, 2.56-2.86]) and urban residence with higher anxiety risk (AHR, 2.15 [95% CI, 2.04-2.28]). In females with IDD, depression and anxiety, respectively, were associated with lower income (AHR, 2.08 [95% CI, 1.86-2.34] and 1.76 [95% CI, 1.59-1.96]) and urban residence (AHR, 2.03 [95% CI, 1.88-2.20] and 1.73 [95% CI, 1.62-1.86]). Mild comorbidity burden was associated with increased risks of depression (AHR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.07-1.31]) and anxiety (AHR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.06-1.27]) for both sexes. Within the IDD cohort, female sex, older age, and lower income status were associated with higher risks of both outcomes (all P &amp;lt; .001 for trend). Conclusions and Relevance This nationwide cohort study of more than 236 000 children and adolescents found that individuals with IDD, particularly males, younger children, and those with mild comorbidity burden, had increased depression and anxiety risks compared with individuals without developmental disorders. These findings underscore the need for targeted screening and interventions tailored to sociodemographic and comorbidity profiles.

item.title: Trends in Ophthalmic Hospital Transfers and Consultations Across US Academic Centers
item.dc:creator: Shu Feng
Karine D. Bojikian
Thellea K. Leveque
Jacquelyn O’Banion
Daniel B. Moore
Donna H. Kim
Andrew T. Melson
Samuel J. Prater
item.description:
Authors: Shu Feng, Karine D. Bojikian, Thellea K. Leveque, Jacquelyn O’Banion, Daniel B. Moore, Donna H. Kim, Andrew T. Melson, Samuel J. Prater, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2640040
Abstract: Importance Academic medical centers increasingly serve as a safety net for urgent and complex ophthalmic conditions, yet trends in the demand for hospital-based ophthalmic services remain poorly characterized. Objective To characterize multi-institutional trends in ophthalmology interhospital transfer requests and emergency department (ED) and inpatient ophthalmology consultation requests (hereafter, consultations) from other departments within the same hospital, such as emergency medicine or internal medicine, at multiple academic medical centers in the US. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective, longitudinal, cohort study involved 14 hospitals affiliated with 10 academic medical centers across multiple geographic regions in the US, representing large urban tertiary referral centers serving diverse catchment populations. Participants were patients for whom ED and inpatient interhospital transfers for ophthalmic care were requested and/or accepted, and patients who received inpatient or ED ophthalmic consultation at participating academic medical centers from 2013 through 2024. Exposure Participating institutions were required to be academic hospitals with resident participation in on-call coverage and to maintain hospital transfer or consultation data from at least 2017 onward, with the earliest beginning in 2013. Main Outcomes and Measures Trends in population-adjusted and hospital volume-adjusted rates of ophthalmology interhospital transfer requests and ED and inpatient ophthalmology consultations. Results A total of 32 131 ophthalmology transfer requests, 23 560 accepted transfers, and 139 356 ophthalmology consultations (83 581 ED and 44 472 inpatient) were recorded across participating hospitals. Transfer requests increased by an aggregate 0.66 (95% CI, 0.51-0.81) per 100 000 state residents per year and accepted transfers by 0.34 per 100 000 state residents per year (95% CI, 0.17-0.51). Among the 7 institutions with consultation data, consultations increased by an aggregate 3.01 per 100 000 state residents per year (95% CI, 2.33-3.69), comprising 2.06 per 100 000 per year for ED consultations (95% CI, 1.51-2.61) and 1.08 per 100 000 per year for inpatient consultations (95% CI, 0.87-1.30). All aggregate trends were significant (false-discovery rate–adjusted P &amp;lt; .001). Conclusions In this cohort study, ophthalmic interhospital transfer requests and inpatient and ED ophthalmology consultations increased substantially across academic medical centers over the study period. These trends suggest growing demand for hospital-based ophthalmic care and increasing strain on ophthalmology hospital coverage, with important implications for workforce sustainability and health system planning.

item.title: A Community-Based Behavioral Intervention and Body Mass Index in School-Aged Children
item.dc:creator: Monica L. Wang
Selenne Alatorre
Aviva G. Schwarz
Janice Weinberg
Linda Sprague Martinez
Jennifer Aldworth
Rabindra Kadel
Milagros C. Rosal
item.description:
Authors: Monica L. Wang, Selenne Alatorre, Aviva G. Schwarz, Janice Weinberg, Linda Sprague Martinez, Jennifer Aldworth, Rabindra Kadel, Milagros C. Rosal, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638188
Abstract: Importance Childhood obesity remains a major concern in the US, with increases in body mass index (BMI) observed during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Scalable behavioral interventions are needed to support obesity prevention in community settings. Objective To evaluate the efficacy of a community-based behavioral intervention (H 2 GO!) on BMI z scores ( z BMIs) among school-aged children. Design, Setting, and Participants This cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted from September 2020 to June 2025 across 11 Boys &amp;amp; Girls Club sites in Massachusetts. Sites were pair-matched and randomized to intervention or usual care condition. Participants included children aged 8 to 13 years and their parents or caregivers. Intervention Twelve group-based sessions delivered in person over 6 weeks by trained Boys &amp;amp; Girls Club staff using behavioral strategies to reduce sugar-sweetened beverage intake and increase water consumption through health sessions, youth-created narratives, and parent-child activities. Comparison sites received usual programming. Main Outcomes and Measures Outcomes were assessed at baseline and at 2, 6, and 12 months using intention-to-treat analyses. The primary outcome was 12-month change from baseline in child z BMI, derived from staff-measured height and weight using standardized protocols. Secondary outcomes included child sugar-sweetened beverage and water intake measured using a validated questionnaire. Results Among 437 child participants (mean [SD] age, 10.1 [1.2] years; 219 girls [50.1%]), 0.2% were American Indian or Alaska Native, 1.8% were Asian, 15.8% were Black or African American, 42.6% were Hispanic or Latino, and 29.5% were White; 297 (68%) were eligible for free or reduced-price lunch. At baseline, 74 children (16.9%) had overweight, and 161 (36.8%) had obesity. From baseline to 12 months, the mean z BMI did not statistically significantly decrease (−0.11 [95% CI, –0.25 to 0.02]) in the intervention group and did not statistically significantly increase (0.08 [95% CI, –0.04 to 0.20]) in the comparison group; however, the estimated between-group difference in the adjusted mean z BMI change from baseline was statistically significant: −0.19 (95% CI, −0.38 to −0.01; P = .04). Between-group differences in sugar-sweetened beverage and water intake were not significant. Conclusions and Relevance In this cluster randomized clinical trial, a community-based behavioral intervention was associated with a statistically significant between-group difference in z BMI change among school-aged children. Findings support the potential of community-based behavioral interventions in obesity prevention. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04265794

item.title: Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity
item.dc:creator: Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley
Rafal Gulej
Zalan Kaposzta
Zsofia Szarvas
Ali Shahriari
Henry Kinnard
Bryan Ticer
Camila B. Pinto
item.description:
Authors: Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. Pinto, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638047
Abstract: Importance Midlife obesity affects nearly half of US adults and is a major risk factor for chronic diseases. Mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to obesity-related endothelial dysfunction and disease risk, highlighting the mitochondria as a potential intervention target. Urolithin A (UA), a polyphenol-derived microbial metabolite and mitophagy activator, is safe and benefits mitochondrial health in humans. Objective To investigate whether supplementation with UA improved peripheral endothelial and cerebrovascular function in middle-aged adults with obesity. Design, Setting, and Participants This was a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial conducted at a single site (University of Oklahoma Health Campus) from October 2023 to May 2025. Middle-aged adults (40-64 years) with a body mass index of 30 or greater were eligible to enroll. Intervention Enrolled participants were randomized 1:1 to receive 1000 mg of UA or placebo for 4 weeks. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was change in brachial artery flow–mediated dilation (FMD) from baseline to end point comparing control and active groups. Secondary outcomes included complementary peripheral endothelial function measures (reactive hyperemia–induced perfusion fold change and acute reperfusion in the dorsal hand and reactive hyperemia index in the fingertips) and cerebrovascular function measures (task-evoked cerebrovascular hemodynamic responses and task performance). Primary analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. Results Overall, 50 participants were included (25 active and 25 control); mean (SD) age was 50.7 (7.1) years, mean (SD) BMI was 38.3 (7.0), and 37 (74%) were female. Mean (SD) follow-up duration was 28 (2) days. Seven participants were lost to follow-up (14% dropout rate). Change in mean (SD) FMD did not differ significantly based on group allocation (control: 0.3% [5.1%]; active: 1.3% [7.6%]). Similarly, there was no significant treatment effect on secondary peripheral endothelial function outcomes. T-contrast maps showed significantly greater task-evoked hemodynamic responses after supplementation with UA relative to placebo (control: mean [SD] β coefficient, −1.43 [5.26]; active: mean [SD] β coefficient, 15.53 [13.02]), while task performance remained unchanged. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of 50 participants, 4 weeks of UA supplementation did not significantly improve peripheral endothelial function in middle-aged adults with obesity. However, supplementation was well tolerated and feasible, and its effect on task-evoked cerebrovascular hemodynamic responses warrants further investigation. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05921266

item.title: Experiences of Mothers Following the Medicaid Postpartum Extension
item.dc:creator: Brittany J. Raffa
Isabella Higgins
Paul Lanier
Samantha S. Schilling
item.description:
Authors: Brittany J. Raffa, Isabella Higgins, Paul Lanier, Samantha S. Schilling
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638838
Abstract: Importance The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 extended postpartum coverage for women eligible for Medicaid for Pregnant Women from 60 days to 12 months. Understanding how mothers experienced the postpartum extension is vital in evaluating this policy change and informing policymakers on how policies aimed at one family member can improve outcomes for the family unit. Objective To describe the experiences of postpartum mothers following the Medicaid postpartum coverage extension in North Carolina from 60 days to 12 months. Design, Setting, and Participants This qualitative study used semistructured interviews of postpartum mothers conducted between April and October 2025 who delivered while enrolled in Medicaid for Pregnant Women in North Carolina. Transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis. Main Outcomes and Measures Themes regarding participant experiences with extended postpartum Medicaid coverage. Results A total of 16 mothers (mean [SD] age, 30.0 [5.6] years; mean [SD] number of living children, 3 [1.6]; mean [SD] age of most recent child, 17.0 [4.8] months) participated. Five themes were identified: (1) confusion around Medicaid coverage, (2) Medicaid facilitates care access, (3) behavioral health services as critical during postpartum period, (4) decreased financial stress and improved family interactions, and (5) Medicaid prevents foregone care. Conclusions and Relevance In this qualitative study of postpartum mothers’ experiences accessing care following the Medicaid postpartum coverage extension, when mothers were aware of the extension, coverage was crucial to meet a variety of postpartum needs, especially behavioral health needs, and had positive effects on the entire family. Increasing engagement with Medicaid beneficiaries and community partners about policy changes is critical for increasing effectiveness. Access to behavioral health services is especially important beyond 12 months post partum.

item.title: Pubertal Testicular Function in Childhood Cancer Survivors and Future Fertility
item.dc:creator: Mikael Koskela
Kathleen Duffin
Melanie Korhonen
Mikko Anttonen
Hanne Frederiksen
Anders Juul
Rod T. Mitchell
Kirsi Jahnukainen
item.description:
Authors: Mikael Koskela, Kathleen Duffin, Melanie Korhonen, Mikko Anttonen, Hanne Frederiksen, Anders Juul, Rod T. Mitchell, Kirsi Jahnukainen
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638294
Abstract: Importance Childhood cancer treatment can result in male infertility. Understanding which patients are at risk of future infertility would facilitate early fertility counseling. Objectives To investigate associations between pubertal reproductive hormone levels and adult gonadal outcomes and cancer treatment exposures. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study was conducted at Helsinki Children’s Hospital among male childhood cancer survivors who received a diagnosis under the age of 17 years between 1964 and 2000, for whom at least 1 reproductive hormone concentration (measured 1982-2017) was available. Data were analyzed from May to December 2025. Exposure Alkylating chemotherapy, quantified using cyclophosphamide equivalent dose (CED), and testicular radiotherapy. Main Outcomes and Measures Serum hormone levels (follicle-stimulating hormone [FSH], luteinizing hormone [LH], or testosterone) were collected at 2-year intervals between ages 12 and 18 years and at age 20 or older; hormone concentrations were converted to age-specific z scores. Data on gonadal outcomes were obtained in adulthood. Results The study included 221 childhood cancer survivors (median age at diagnosis, 6.0 years [IQR, 3.2-11.7 years]). FSH showed a dose-dependent pattern with testicular radiotherapy, with elevated FSH z scores seen from age 12 years among patients who received more than 1 Gy of testicular radiotherapy. Compared with the group that received less than 4 g/m 2 CED (median FSH z score, 0.1; IQR, −1.2 to 1.2) at age 18 years, higher FSH z scores occurred among patients who received 4 to less than 12 g/m 2 CED (median FSH z score, 1.4; IQR, 0.5-2.6; P = .04) or received 12 g/m 2 or more CED (median FSH z score, 1.6; IQR, 0.7-2.5; P = .007). There was evidence of normalization at age 20 years or older for patients who received 4 to less than 12 g/m 2 CED (median FSH z score, 0.7; IQR, −0.6 to 1.7) but not those who received 12 g/m 2 or more CED (median FSH z score, 1.7; IQR, 0.9-2.5). The highest FSH z score at age 14 to 16 years was associated with azoospermia in adulthood, with an optimal cutoff corresponding to 11.2 IU/L at age 14 years and 12.5 IU/L at age 16 years (area under the curve, 0.87). Elevated LH z scores occurred from age 12 years onward among patients receiving more than 14 Gy of radiotherapy, but exposure to high CED was not associated with impaired Leydig cell function. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of male patients treated for childhood cancer, gonadotrophin levels during puberty were associated with future testicular function. Impairment of testicular function after radiotherapy persisted into adulthood, while there was evidence of recovery after alkylating chemotherapy. The results suggest increased sensitivity of the Sertoli cell–germ cell compartment compared with Leydig cells. These findings can be used to guide reproductive counseling for male survivors of childhood cancer.

item.title: Roxadustat Treatment After PCI Among Patients With ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction
item.dc:creator: Weiwei Quan
Yueying Wang
Min Zhang
Tianqi Zhu
Jinzhou Zhu
Xiaoqun Wang
Zhengbin Zhu
Run Du
item.description:
Authors: Weiwei Quan, Yueying Wang, Min Zhang, Tianqi Zhu, Jinzhou Zhu, Xiaoqun Wang, Zhengbin Zhu, Run Du, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2637953
Abstract: Importance Preclinical studies suggest that stabilization of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) may attenuate reperfusion injury. Objective To determine whether oral roxadustat, a HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor, reduced infarct size when administered after reperfusion among patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Design, Setting, and Participants This phase 2, open-label, randomized clinical trial—Effect of Roxadustat in Acute Myocardial Infarction (ROXAMI)—enrolled adults with STEMI undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) at a single tertiary medical center between April 1, 2021, and March 31, 2024, with follow-up through 1 year. Interventions Oral roxadustat (100 mg, 3 times per week for 2 weeks), initiated within 2 hours after primary PCI, or standard care alone. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary end point was infarct size as a percentage of the left ventricle at 30 days measured by late gadolinium enhancement on [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Prespecified secondary end points included major adverse cardiovascular events, myocardial injury markers, echocardiographic parameters, and myocardial fibroblast activation parameters on [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET and MRI. The primary efficacy analysis for infarct size was conducted in the modified intention-to-treat population. Results Among 158 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 63.6 [11.0] years; 133 men [84.2%]; 79 randomized to each group), 148 (93.7%; 72 roxadustat and 76 control) had evaluable imaging for the primary outcome. For the primary end point, mean (SD) infarct size did not significantly differ between the roxadustat and control groups (23.3% [12.2%] vs 22.0% [12.2%]; mean difference, 1.3 percentage points; 95% CI, −2.7 to 5.3 percentage points; P = .51). Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 3 of 79 patients (3.8%) in the roxadustat group and 7 of 79 (8.9%) in the control group (hazard ratio, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.11-1.63; P = .21). In multiplicity-unadjusted secondary analyses, adjusted between-group differences at 12 months were 2.9 percentage points (95% CI, 0.4-5.3 percentage points; P = .02) for the change in left ventricular ejection fraction (mean [SD]: roxadustat, 3.4% [0.9%] vs control, 0.5% [0.9%]) and −4.5 mL/m 2 (95% CI, −8.9 to −0.1 mL/m 2 ; P = .045) for left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (mean [SD]: roxadustat, 1.2 [1.6] mL/m 2 vs control, 5.7 [1.6] mL/m 2 ). The incidence of prespecified safety end points did not differ between the roxadustat and control groups. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of patients with STEMI, roxadustat administration after PCI did not significantly reduce infarct size at 30 days compared with control. Secondary ventricular remodeling findings were exploratory and require confirmation. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04803864

item.title: Recent and Cumulative Cannabis Use and Sleep in Middle-Aged Adults

item.description:
Authors: Thanh-Huyen T. Vu, Kristen L. Knutson, Reto Auer, Julian Jakob, Donald M. Lloyd-Jones, Mercedes R. Carnethon
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638303
Abstract: Importance Cannabis is widely used and often promoted as a sleep aid, but evidence of its long-term implications for sleep is limited. Objective To examine the associations of cumulative cannabis exposure from young adulthood to middle age and recent cannabis use with objective and subjective sleep outcomes in middle age. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study analyzed data from the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, including 35 years of follow-up through the year-35 examination (conducted in 2020 to 2022), and the CARDIA Year-35 Sleep Ancillary Study. Analyses were conducted from January 15 to July 15, 2026. Exposures Cumulative cannabis use (calculated in cannabis-years, with 1 cannabis-year equating to 365 days of use) and recent cannabis use (defined as past 30-day use vs former use and never use). Main Outcomes and Measures Objective sleep was assessed using data from 7-day wrist actigraphy, and subjective sleep was assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Primary outcomes and measures were objective sleep duration (categorized as short [&amp;lt;6 hours], optimal [6-8 hours], or long [&amp;gt;8 hours]), sleep percentage (defined as percentage of time asleep; low percentage: &amp;lt;85%), sleep fragmentation (defined as the index of restlessness during sleep; high fragmentation: highest quartile), and wakefulness after sleep onset (WASO; prolonged WASO: ≥30 minutes) and subjective sleep quality (PSQI score and poor sleep quality: PSQI &amp;gt;5). Results A total of 1266 participants (891 with objective and 1128 with subjective sleep data) were analyzed. Among the 891 participants with objective sleep data, the mean (SD) age at the year-35 examination was 60.7 (3.6) years; the cohort included 564 females (63.3%) and 365 Black (41.0%) and 526 White (59.0%) participants. After multivariable adjustment, each additional cannabis-year was associated with higher odds of low sleep percentage (odds ratio [OR], 1.10; 95% CI, 1.06-1.14), high sleep fragmentation (OR, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.01-1.08), and prolonged WASO (OR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.10-1.34). Compared with participants with former use and never use status, those with recent use had higher odds of low sleep percentage, high fragmentation, prolonged WASO, and long (vs optimal) sleep duration (eg, vs never use, prolonged WASO: OR, 3.23 [95% CI, 1.44-7.27]; long sleep duration: OR, 4.60 [95% CI, 1.81-11.70]). Cannabis use was not associated with subjective sleep quality. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, both cumulative use and recent cannabis use were associated with poorer objective sleep quality, although no association with self-reported sleep quality was found. These findings underscore the importance of assessing both subjective and objective sleep and suggest potential adverse association between long-term recreational cannabis exposure and midlife sleep health.

item.description:
Authors: Yannine Estrada, Alyssa Lozano, Beck Graefe, Tae Kyoung Lee, Elliott Mitrani, Padideh Lovan, Maria Isabel Tapia, Tatiana Perrino, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2637908
Abstract: Importance Culturally tailored, evidence-based family interventions that can be effectively delivered within pediatric primary care settings may provide a scalable approach for preventing risk behaviors among Hispanic adolescents. Objective To evaluate whether the online eHealth Familias Unidas Primary Care (eHealth FUPC) program reduced drug use and increased condom use in Hispanic youth and to examine family functioning as a mediator. Design, Setting, and Participants This randomized clinical trial included 5 follow-up visits across 36 months from April 18, 2017, to December 18, 2022, at 15 pediatric primary care clinics. Participants included Hispanic youth aged 12 to 16 years and a legal guardian. Data were analyzed from January 31, 2023, to August 21, 2024. Intervention Participants were randomized 1:1 to the intervention, consisting of 8 video group sessions for parents and 4 online, facilitator-guided family sessions for parents and adolescents for a total intervention duration of approximately 12 weeks. Interventionists included pediatric primary care personnel. Main Outcomes and Measures The co-primary outcomes were past 90-day drug use, condom use, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Secondary outcomes included initiation of alcohol use, initiation of hard drug use (ie, lysergic acid diethylamide, phencyclidine, ecstasy [MDMA], psilocybin mushrooms), and family functioning. STI was changed to a secondary outcome after data collection was discontinued because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Results A total of 456 dyads of adolescents (mean [SD] age, 13.9 [1.4] years; 241 [52.9%] female) and parents or caregivers (mean [SD] age, 43.2 [6.6] years; 424 [93.0%] female) were included in the primary intention-to-treat analyses (225 in the eHealth FUPC intervention and 231 in treatment as usual). A total of 356 families (78.1%) completed the final assessment. eHealth FUPC effects were found for past 90-day drug use trajectories (unstandardized b [SE] = −0.70 [0.70]; incidence rate ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, −0.84 to −0.55; P &amp;lt; .001), alcohol initiation (χ 2 1 = 3.85; P = .05; Cramer V = 0.10), and hard drug use (χ 2 1 = 4.14; P = .04; Cramer V = 0.10), with less initiation for eHealth FUPC. Intervention effects were not found for condom use, condom use trajectory, or family functioning. Conclusions and Relevance In this randomized clinical trial of the eHealth FUPC intervention, compared with treatment as usual, the experimental condition showed reduced drug use across time and prevented youths from initiating alcohol and hard drug use. No intervention effects were found for condom use. Whether behavioral preventive evidence-based interventions such as eHealth FUPC can be maintained in organizations such as primary care clinics should be further researched. item.title: Disparities in Autism Spectrum Disorder and Perinatal Risk Factors
item.dc:creator: Francesca del Giorgio
Bénédicte Driollet
Emmalin Buajitti
Asma Ahmed
Jennifer A. Hutcheon
Laura Rosella
Seungmi Yang
item.description:
Authors: Francesca del Giorgio, Bénédicte Driollet, Emmalin Buajitti, Asma Ahmed, Jennifer A. Hutcheon, Laura Rosella, Seungmi Yang
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2637174
Abstract: Importance In universal health care settings, trends in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnosis remain poorly characterized, yet are critical for identifying inequities that persist despite more equitable health care access. Objective To describe temporal trends in ASD diagnosis and in perinatal risk factors for ASD across maternal socioeconomic and immigration factors. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a population-based retrospective cohort study of children born in Ontario, Canada (2002-2020), linked to maternal health, immigration, and census data. Children were followed up from age 1 year until ASD diagnosis, death, out-migration, or April 2020. Data analysis was performed between August 2024 and March 2026. Exposures Maternal socioeconomic indicators (area-level deprivation, ethnic diversity, income, Ontario Drug Benefit enrollment, and rural vs urban residence) and immigration characteristics (immigration status, category, time since immigration, region of origin, and country income level). Perinatal risk factors included maternal diabetes, maternal age 35 years or older, severe maternal morbidity, and prematurity. Main Outcomes and Measures ASD was identified using a validated administrative algorithm. Incidence rates were calculated per 10 000 person-years and cumulative incidence per 1000 live births at 8 years. Temporal trends were estimated using negative binomial regression with interaction terms between birth year and covariates. Results Of 2 319 302 children (1 188 270 male [51.2%]), 29 374 (1.3%) met ASD criteria, with 80.0% (23 068 children) receiving a diagnosis by age 8 years and 78.5% of cases (23 071 cases) occurring in male children. Diagnosis increased by 10% per birth cohort (95% CI, 10%-11%). Disparities in ASD diagnosis by socioeconomic and immigration characteristics widened across birth cohorts: by the 2012 birth cohort, diagnosis was 2.2-fold (95% CI, 2.0-2.4–fold) higher in the most vs least deprived neighborhoods, 2.0-fold (95% CI, 1.8-2.2–fold) higher in the most vs least ethnically diverse areas, and lower in rural vs urban regions. Diagnosis was 1.4-fold (95% CI, 1.3-1.5–fold) higher among children of immigrant mothers, with the highest rates among mothers from low- and middle-income regions. Diabetes during pregnancy, severe maternal morbidity, and prematurity were more common in marginalized populations, with disparities in maternal diabetes widening over time. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study of more than 2.3 million mother-child pairs, ASD diagnoses occurred disproportionately among children from socioeconomically disadvantaged and immigrant families, with disparities widening over time. The higher prevalence of maternal diabetes, obstetric complications, and prematurity in these populations may have contributed to these differences.

item.title: Maternal Influenza Infection During Pregnancy and Neuropsychiatric Disorders in Offspring
item.dc:creator: Jaehyun Kong
Seohyun Hong
Hyesu Jo
Jaeyu Park
Kyeongeun Kim
Dongjin Yeo
Hyunjee Kim
Tae Hyeon Kim
item.description:
Authors: Jaehyun Kong, Seohyun Hong, Hyesu Jo, Jaeyu Park, Kyeongeun Kim, Dongjin Yeo, Hyunjee Kim, Tae Hyeon Kim, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2637902
Abstract: Importance Evidence on maternal influenza infection during pregnancy and offspring neuropsychiatric risk remains inconsistent and limited by methodologic concerns. Objective To evaluate the association of maternal influenza infection during pregnancy and offspring neuropsychiatric risk. Design, Setting, and Participants This binational cohort study included mother-child pairs from the National Health Insurance Service birth cohort in South Korea (discovery cohort) and the JMDC (previously Japan Medical Data Center) birth cohort in Japan (replication cohort). Children born between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2017, were included in the study and followed up until December 31, 2023. Exposure A first recorded maternal influenza diagnosis during pregnancy. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was first postnatal diagnosis of any neuropsychiatric disorder in offspring, including severe neuropsychiatric disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting was applied to adjust for confounding. Weighted Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (AHRs) and 95% CIs. Subgroup analyses were conducted by trimester and season of infection, and sibling-comparison analyses used exposure-discordant sibling pairs. Data analysis was performed from September 2025 to July 2026. Results The discovery cohort included 2 564 435 mother-child pairs (mean [SD] maternal age, 31.9 [4.1] years; 1 293 773 [50.5%] male offspring), of whom 35 973 (1.4%) were exposed to maternal influenza during pregnancy. The replication cohort included 181 681 pairs (92 738 [51.0%] male offspring), of whom 11 198 (6.2%) were exposed. In stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting–based analyses, maternal influenza infection was associated with an increased risk of any neuropsychiatric disorder in the discovery cohort (AHR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.04-1.14) and replication cohort (AHR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.02-1.19). Sibling-comparison analyses included 33 191 and 7842 mother-child pairs in the discovery and replication cohorts, respectively; there was not a statistically significant association in the discovery cohort (AHR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.89-1.09) and replication cohort (AHR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.88-1.22). Conclusions and Relevance In this binational cohort study of mother-child pairs in South Korea and Japan, the modest population-level association between maternal influenza infection during pregnancy and the risk of any neuropsychiatric disorder in offspring was attenuated and not statistically significant in sibling-comparison analyses in either cohort. These findings suggest that familial factors may account for the association observed in the population-level analysis.

item.title: Development and Validation of a Tool to Measure Documented Health Care Encounter Time
item.dc:creator: Ronald Chow
Sarah Bayrakdarian
Olivera Gojsevic
Emily MacMillan
Tracy Balboni
Joanne Bowen
Eduardo Bruera
Raymond J. Chan
item.description:
Authors: Ronald Chow, Sarah Bayrakdarian, Olivera Gojsevic, Emily MacMillan, Tracy Balboni, Joanne Bowen, Eduardo Bruera, Raymond J. Chan, et al.
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638034
Abstract: Importance Time toxicity, defined as the time patients spend receiving cancer treatment and interacting with health care systems, is an emerging treatment-related burden. Existing studies typically quantify time toxicity using health care contact days, which may inadequately capture patient burden because encounters of different durations are weighted equally. Objective To develop and internally validate the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC) Time Intensity and Measurement of Encounters (TIME) tool, a standardized medical record abstraction instrument for measuring documented health care encounter time. Design, Setting, and Participants This multiphase mixed-methods prognostic study, including tool development, was conducted from March to May 2026, through a 3-round international consensus process involving 16 oncology trialists from 9 countries and internal validation using electronic medical records from a cohort of patients with prostate cancer treated at a tertiary cancer center in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Validation compared standardized abstraction using the MASCC TIME tool with prior unstructured medical record abstraction across 367 health care encounters. Main Outcomes and Measures Content validity, extraction accuracy compared with investigator consensus review, interrater reliability assessed using the Gwet agreement coefficient 1 (AC1) and percentage agreement, and abstraction feasibility. Results Sixteen oncology trialists participated in tool development. The final tool included 8 variables: encounter start date, start time, end date, end time, purpose, planned or unplanned status, mode of contact, and primary clinician. All variables achieved a content validity ratio of 1.0. Accuracy of medical record extraction increased from 31% (95% CI, 28%-35%) to 90% (95% CI, 87%-93%) without the tool to 66% (95% CI, 62%-69%) to 99% (95% CI, 99%-100%) with the tool, with absolute differences of 2 percentage points (95% CI, −1 to 5 percentage points) to 35 percentage points (95% CI, 30 to 40 percentage points); 7 of 8 variables demonstrated statistically significant increases with the tool. Percentage agreement between abstractors increased from 31% to 82% without the tool to 42% to 99% with the tool, while the Gwet AC1 increased from −0.24 to 0.87 without the tool to 0.14 to 0.99 with the tool. Mean abstraction time decreased from 10 to 5 minutes per encounter. Conclusions and Relevance In this prognostic study of the MASCC TIME tool, it was found to be associated with excellent content validity, improved accuracy, high interrater reliability, and acceptable feasibility for standardized measurement of documented health care encounter time. Standardized assessment of time toxicity may improve comparability across oncology studies and support more rigorous evaluation of health care–related burden in cancer research.

item.dc:creator: Christie Rampersad
Ian Tatt Liew
Kuan Liu
Georgina L. Irish
Philip A. Clayton
Greg Knoll
Kyla Naylor
S. Joseph Kim
item.description:
Authors: Christie Rampersad, Ian Tatt Liew, Kuan Liu, Georgina L. Irish, Philip A. Clayton, Greg Knoll, Kyla Naylor, S. Joseph Kim
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2637964
Abstract: Importance Preemptive kidney transplantation (before dialysis) is promoted as optimal therapy for kidney failure, yet evidence of a true survival advantage remains uncertain due to confounding, selection, and lead-time biases. Objective To estimate the associations of preemptive vs nonpreemptive kidney transplantation with mortality and graft outcomes using a target trial emulation among transplant recipients. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study used data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients, a nationwide registry of all US kidney transplant centers, from January 1, 2005, to November 30, 2023. Adult first kidney-alone transplant recipients with recorded wait-time start at an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 20 mL/min/1.73 m 2 or less were included. Groups were balanced using stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) to emulate randomization across demographic, clinical, and socioeconomic factors identified by a directed acyclic graph. Analyses were conducted from July to October 2025. Exposures Preemptive vs nonpreemptive kidney transplantation, defined by dialysis before transplant. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were all-cause graft failure, death-censored graft failure, and delayed graft function. IPTW was incorporated for baseline confounding to address selection bias. Weighted Kaplan-Meier curves estimated survival differences; hazard ratios (HRs) and odds ratios (ORs) were derived from weighted left-truncated Cox proportional hazards (to address lead-time bias) and logistic regression models, respectively. Results Among 32 770 recipients (15 894 [48.5%] preemptive [mean (SD) age, 53.7 (13.1) years; 7007 (44.1%) female] and 16 876 [51.5%] nonpreemptive [mean (SD) age, 54.5 (13.0) years; 6978 (41.3%) female]) with more than 265 369 person-years of follow-up, 6827 deaths occurred. Preemptive transplantation showed no mortality benefit (HR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.96-1.07). The weighted survival differences were approximately 1% to 2% annually. Preemptive transplantation was associated with lower odds of delayed graft function (OR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.64-0.72) and reduced risk of death-censored graft failure (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.74-0.88), an association largely attenuated after adjustment for delayed graft function. There was no association with all-cause graft failure (HR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.91-1.00). Conclusions and Relevance In this study, preemptive transplantation was not associated with improved patient survival but was associated with lower rates of delayed graft function and death-censored graft failure. Findings challenge presumed survival advantages and suggest preemptive strategies should focus on preventing early graft dysfunction and optimizing use of high-risk kidneys rather than expected mortality benefit.

item.title: LGBTQ+ Disparities in Food Insecurity, Food Assistance Use, and Barriers to Food Assistance
item.dc:creator: Austin R. Waters
Lauren G. Fiechtner
Meghan E. Perkins
Man Luo
Michele F. Schuckel
Catherine D’Amato
Brittany M. Charlton
item.description:
Authors: Austin R. Waters, Lauren G. Fiechtner, Meghan E. Perkins, Man Luo, Michele F. Schuckel, Catherine D’Amato, Brittany M. Charlton
Journal: JAMA Network Open; Volume: 9; Issue: 10; Pages: e2638129
Abstract: Importance Food insecurity disproportionately affects lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ+) adults, yet population-based data on disparities in food assistance use and barriers to accessing services remain limited. Objectives To estimate the prevalence of food insecurity and food assistance program use among LGBTQ+ adults in Massachusetts from 2022 to 2024 and identify LGBTQ+-specific barriers to assistance. Design, Setting, and Participants This repeated cross-sectional analysis used 2022 to 2024 data from the Massachusetts Statewide Food Access Survey, an annual online survey conducted by the Greater Boston Food Bank and Mass General Brigham. Exposure LGBTQ+ identity, defined using a 2-step measure of sexual orientation and gender. Main Outcomes and Measures Food insecurity, measured using the 10-item US Department of Agriculture Food Security Survey Module; food pantry and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) use; and barriers to food assistance access. Weighted prevalence estimates and adjusted prevalence ratios with 95% CIs were calculated by LGBTQ+ status. Results The sample included 9174 Massachusetts adults (10.4%-12.8% LGBTQ+ across survey years). The prevalence of food insecurity increased significantly from 2022 to 2024 among both non-LGBTQ+ adults (29.8% [95% CI, 27.7%-32.0%] to 33.3% [95% CI, 31.3%-35.3%]) and LGBTQ+ adults (43.7% [95% CI, 37.7%-49.9%] to 54.9% [95% CI, 48.5%-61.1%]). Food pantry and SNAP use among LGBTQ+ adults remained stable over time. Among LGBTQ+ nonusers of food pantries in 2024, the most common barriers to use were wanting to be self-reliant (49.4% [95% CI, 41.6%-57.4%]), embarrassment (37.4% [95% CI, 30.1%-45.2%]), and fear of being identified as a pantry user (35.6% [95% CI, 28.6%-43.3%]); all barriers increased over time and were more commonly reported than among non-LGBTQ+ adults. Common barriers to SNAP use among LGBTQ+ adults in 2024 included wanting to be self-reliant (52.7% [95% CI, 43.4%-61.8%]), concern about taking benefits from someone with more need (44.6% [95% CI, 35.8%-53.7%]), and not knowing how to apply (26.0% [95% CI, 18.5%-35.1%]). In 2024, LGBTQ+ adults frequently endorsed grocery gift cards (42.5% [95% CI, 36.6%-48.7%]), home delivery (42.4% [95% CI, 36.4%-48.6%]), and online ordering (34.0% [95% CI, 28.5%-39.9%]) as strategies to increase pantry use. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional study of food insecurity in Massachusetts, over half of LGBTQ+ adults experienced food insecurity in 2024, alongside barriers to food assistance use. Findings highlight the need for multilevel, community–co-created interventions to reduce disparities among LGBTQ+ individuals in food insecurity and improve equitable access to food assistance.
